stories.name: Inside Constitutional AI: harmlessness from a list of principles
stories.intro:
By 2022 the recipe for training a helpful assistant was settled: collect human preferences, fit a preference model, let reinforcement learning optimize against it. But the harmlessness half of those preferences was producing assistants that dodged hard questions instead of answering them, and every fix seemed to require more human labels. This paper asks whether the harmlessness labels can be replaced by something smaller and more legible: a short list of written principles.

The chapters follow the paper's own order: the tension that motivates it, the supervised stage where the model critiques and rewrites its own worst answers, the RL stage where a model supplies the preference labels, and the measurements behind the claim that the tradeoff between helping and refusing actually moved.
stories.narrative: Constitutional AI trains a harmless assistant with no human harmlessness labels at all: a constitution of written principles steers the model to critique and revise its own harmful outputs in the supervised stage, then steers a feedback model to label harmlessness preferences in the RL stage — and the resulting RL-CAI model is rated both more harmless and less evasive than models trained on human harm labels.

children.name: The problem: harmlessness that learns to hide
children.narrative: The paper opens on a failure of its authors' own prior work: reinforcement learning from human feedback can make an assistant harmless, but the cheapest route to harmlessness is refusal, and crowdworkers rewarding harmlessness in isolation had produced models that met sensitive questions with boilerplate (constitutional-ai, §"1.1 Motivations", p. 2). The motivations section frames the fix as a supervision-scaling problem: as capabilities grow, human oversight becomes the bottleneck, so let AI systems carry part of it (constitutional-ai, §"Scaling Supervision", p. 2). Before staking anything on that idea, the paper checks its feasibility — language models can already tell helpful, honest, and harmless responses apart, and get better at it with scale. The one input no principle can generate, harmful prompts, comes from human red teaming, the same crowdworker machinery the rest of the paper works to move beyond.

children.name: The tension the paper starts from
children.narrative: Helpfulness training and harmlessness training pull against each other: assistants trained to help more will help with harm, and assistants trained against harm learn to disengage. The whole paper is an attempt to show this tradeoff is not fixed (constitutional-ai, §"1.1 Motivations", p. 2).

children.name: Evasiveness, the named failure
children.narrative: The paper gives the failure a name: canned refusals that score as harmless while giving the user nothing. Naming it lets the paper measure it, and later tune its Elo evaluations to penalize it (constitutional-ai, §"A Harmless but Non-Evasive (Still Helpful) Assistant", p. 4).

children.name: Scaling supervision
children.narrative: Inherited from the 2016 agenda as an open problem, scalable oversight acquires an operational reading here: use AI to supervise AI at exactly the points where human labeling cannot keep up (constitutional-ai, §"Scaling Supervision", p. 2).

children.name: First, check that the judge can judge
children.narrative: Before delegating harmlessness judgments to a model, the paper verifies that models can make them: on binary helpful-honest-harmless comparisons, identification accuracy climbs steadily with model size (constitutional-ai, §"2 Evaluating the Potential for AI Supervision of HHH", p. 6).

children.name: Where the harmful prompts come from
children.narrative: Every stage downstream trains or evaluates on adversarial prompts gathered by human [[red-teaming|red teaming]]; this theme covers that sourcing, the appendix evaluations built from the same transcripts, and the [[automated-red-teaming|automated version]] the paper points toward.

children.name: Act one: the model rewrites its own answers
children.narrative: The supervised stage deliberately starts from the most dangerous model available: a helpful-only RLHF assistant that responds to red-team prompts with genuinely harmful content. Each such response is handed back to the model along with a principle sampled from the constitution — first critique your answer against the principle, then revise it to remove the harm, possibly several times over (constitutional-ai, §"3 Constitutional AI: Critiques, Revisions, and Supervised Learning", p. 7). A pretrained model finetuned on the revisions, with helpfulness samples mixed in so it does not forget how to answer, becomes SL-CAI: already less harmful, and close enough to the target behavior that the RL stage will not have to travel far. An ablation asks whether the critique step earns its keep, and the answer turns out to depend on scale.

children.name: The method, gathered in one place
children.narrative: The theme walks the whole supervised machinery: the constitution's two principle sets, the [[sl-cai-few-shot-examples|few-shot examples]] that keep the critique and revision roles from blurring, and the ablations behind each design choice.

children.name: Start from the helpful, harmful model
children.narrative: The pipeline begins from a helpful-only RLHF model precisely because it answers red-team prompts with usable harm — you cannot revise a refusal (constitutional-ai, §"1.4 Models and Data", p. 6).

children.name: The constitution
children.narrative: Sixteen critique-revision instruction pairs for the supervised stage ([[sl-cai-principles]]) and sixteen comparison principles for RL ([[rl-cai-principles]]): the entire human contribution to harmlessness, small enough to read in minutes (constitutional-ai, §"1.2 The Constitutional AI Approach", p. 5).

children.name: Critique, then revise
children.narrative: The loop at the heart of the supervised stage: the model states how its response violates a sampled principle, then rewrites the response to remove the harm; revisions can be chained, though most of the benefit arrives with the first.

children.name: SL-CAI, the halfway model
children.narrative: Finetuning on revised responses plus helpfulness samples produces SL-CAI — not the finished model but the launchpad, built so that RL starts near the target distribution (constitutional-ai, §"3.2 Datasets and Training", p. 8).

children.name: Are critiques necessary?
children.narrative: Skipping the critique and revising directly works nearly as well at 52B parameters but measurably worse at smaller scales; the paper keeps the critique for transparency as much as for performance (constitutional-ai, §"3.5 Are Critiques Necessary?", p. 10).

children.name: Act two: preference labels without a human labeler
children.narrative: The RL stage is deliberately unoriginal: the same preference-model-plus-RL recipe as standard RLHF, with one substitution — the harmlessness comparisons in the preference-model training set are labeled by a model instead of by crowdworkers (constitutional-ai, §"4 Constitutional AI: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback", p. 10). Making a plain pretrained language model into a trustworthy labeler is the chapter's real work: a multiple-choice format whose answer probabilities become soft labels, a freshly sampled principle for each comparison ([[ensembling-principles|principle ensembling]]), [[chain-of-thought-prompting|chain-of-thought]] reasoning that improves the judgments but overshoots into overconfidence, and [[label-clamping|clamped labels]] to pull it back. Helpfulness labels stay human; the resulting hybrid preference model rewards a policy that begins as SL-CAI and ends as RL-CAI.

children.name: Engineering the labeler
children.narrative: The full chain of prompting and calibration choices — the comparison format, [[lets-think-step-by-step-prompt|the step-by-step trigger]], [[rl-cai-cot-prompts|hand-written chain-of-thought prompts]], and the [[model-calibration|calibration]] the whole scheme leans on — that turns log-probabilities into preference labels.

children.name: RLAIF, the substitution named
children.narrative: The paper's most exportable idea, stated in its first paragraph: RLHF with the human preference labeler replaced by an AI one, for the harmlessness half of the data (constitutional-ai, §"Abstract", p. 1).

children.name: The feedback model
children.narrative: A pretrained model, not a finetuned specialist: shown the conversation, a principle, and two candidate responses, its normalized answer probabilities become the label (constitutional-ai, §"4.1 Method", p. 10).

children.name: The A-or-B question
children.narrative: The load-bearing interface: framing the harmlessness judgment as a multiple-choice question is what lets calibrated log-probabilities stand in for a crowdworker's click (constitutional-ai, §"4.1 Method", p. 10).

children.name: A hybrid preference model
children.narrative: Human helpfulness comparisons and AI harmlessness comparisons train a single preference model — the pipeline's quiet acknowledgment that only one of its two label streams has been automated (constitutional-ai, §"1.2 The Constitutional AI Approach", p. 5).

children.name: RL-CAI, the finished model
children.narrative: The final policy: RL against the hybrid preference model, starting from the SL-CAI snapshot. Everything the paper claims is measured on this model and its chain-of-thought variant (constitutional-ai, §"4 Constitutional AI: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback", p. 10).

children.name: The verdict: a moved frontier, and a familiar failure
children.narrative: The headline result is plotted as crowdworker Elo scores: RL-CAI is rated as harmless as the human-feedback HH model while staying markedly more helpful, which the paper reads as a Pareto improvement — the frontier moved outward, not a new point on the old curve (constitutional-ai, §"1.1 Motivations", p. 3). The result is built as much from redesigning what gets rewarded and scored as from any change to the algorithm, an arc the wiki traces edge by edge in [[evasiveness-empirical-arc|one connective thread]]. A second instrument, the absolute harmfulness score, cross-checks the comparisons on an independent scale. The paper is also candid about what over-optimizing its own reward does — trained too long, RL-CAI turns boilerplate and accusatory, Goodhart's law surfacing inside the very pipeline built to escape a different Goodhart failure (constitutional-ai, §"4.3 Main Results", p. 12). The future-work list closes the loop: with labels this cheap, keeping the preference model fresh stops being bottlenecked on people.

children.name: The tradeoff, measured
children.narrative: The theme assembles the full empirical apparatus behind the paper's central claim: the two RLHF baselines, the Elo curves, and where RL-CAI lands relative to both.

children.name: Elo as the measuring stick
children.narrative: Crowdworker pairwise preferences over model snapshots become Elo ratings for helpfulness and harmlessness separately — and the harmlessness instructions were deliberately tuned so that evasion loses points (constitutional-ai, §"3.3 Main Results", p. 8).

children.name: The frontier claim
children.narrative: The paper's strongest sentence: constitutional RL is both more helpful and more harmless than its RLHF baseline — an outward shift of the frontier rather than movement along it (constitutional-ai, §"1.1 Motivations", p. 3).

children.name: A second, absolute instrument
children.narrative: A 0-4 harmfulness scale predicted by a separately finetuned model gives the relative Elo picture an absolute cross-check; the two instruments broadly agree, which is the point of running both (constitutional-ai, §"4.5 Absolute Harmfulness Score", p. 14).

children.name: Goodhart, again
children.narrative: Over-train against the preference model and RL-CAI grows harsh and accusatory toward harmless-seeming prompts: the 2016 law showing up empirically inside the 2022 pipeline (constitutional-ai, §"4.3 Main Results", p. 12).

children.name: What cheap labels unlock next
children.narrative: Named as future work: with AI-generated labels, continually refitting the preference model on the current policy's outputs becomes automatable rather than a crowdsourcing project (constitutional-ai, §"6.1 Future Directions", p. 15).

stories.name: Constitutional AI across the corpus: the pipeline inherited, the labeler replaced
stories.intro:
Constitutional AI is the youngest paper in this corpus, and one of its best connected: among the four, only the 2017 preference-learning paper touches more cross-paper edges. Almost nothing in its training pipeline is new — the reward model, the RL loop, and the comparison format all arrive intact from earlier papers. What is new is exactly one substitution, and reading it against the corpus makes the substitution easy to see.

The chapters move outward one paper at a time: first InstructGPT, whose pipeline it inherits nearly whole; then the 2017 preference-learning paper, whose mechanism reaches it one step removed; then the 2016 agenda, whose open problem it carries furthest; and finally the corpus-wide motifs in which this paper is the newest instance.
stories.narrative: Read against the rest of the corpus, Constitutional AI is an extension, not a departure: it takes the InstructGPT-style RLHF pipeline whole — preference model, RL loop, comparison data — and swaps out exactly one part, the human harmlessness labeler, while its debts to 2017 and 2016 run through that inherited pipeline rather than around it.

children.name: InstructGPT: the pipeline it inherits, minus one part
children.narrative: Constitutional AI never argues with InstructGPT; it presupposes it. The three-step recipe arrives intact, along with the helpful-honest-harmless vocabulary for saying what the training is for. The change is confined to a single interface: where InstructGPT's preference model consumes crowdworker harmlessness comparisons, CAI's consumes a feedback model's. The two papers also share a failure axis — InstructGPT's [[excessive-hedging|over-hedging]] and CAI's [[evasiveness]] are the same Goodhart pattern surfacing on opposite halves of the same objective, and in both cases the effective fix lived in the labels, not the optimizer.

children.name: The surgical swap
children.narrative: The thread that states this paper's relationship to InstructGPT most precisely: at stage after stage, an AI process replaces a human one at exactly the point where human throughput was the bottleneck, and nothing around it changes.

children.name: RLHF becomes RLAIF: one part changes
children.narrative: The single edge that summarizes the whole relationship: preference-model training and the RL loop are untouched; only the source of the harmlessness labels changes.

children.name: RLHF, the shared chassis
children.narrative: The paradigm itself lives in three papers: proved out in 2017, industrialized by InstructGPT, and extended here until the human in the acronym is only half true (constitutional-ai, §"1 Introduction", p. 2).

children.name: A shared definition of good
children.narrative: Both 2022 papers inherit the same three-word target — helpful, honest, harmless — which is what makes their results directly comparable (constitutional-ai, §"1 Introduction", p. 2).

children.name: Hedging and evasion, mirror failures
children.narrative: InstructGPT's models hedge on easy questions; CAI's baselines refuse hard ones. Read together, the two failures are one phenomenon: a policy over-satisfying the easiest-to-score half of its objective.

children.name: The fix was in the labels
children.narrative: InstructGPT's KL penalty constrains the optimizer, but evasiveness was never an optimizer problem: CAI's fix went upstream, into what the labels — human or AI — actually reward.

children.name: 2017: the mechanism, one paper removed
children.narrative: Constitutional AI's relationship to Deep RL from Human Preferences is mediated: nearly everything it takes from 2017 — Bradley-Terry preference fitting, the comparison as the atomic unit of feedback, the reward model itself — arrives already industrialized by InstructGPT. But a few threads run direct. The Elo framing the 2017 paper used only as an explanatory analogy becomes CAI's primary measurement instrument. And the 2017 practice neither 2022 paper could afford to keep — continually refreshing the reward model with new human comparisons — reappears on CAI's future-work list, newly automatable now that labels no longer cost human hours.

children.name: An analogy becomes an instrument
children.narrative: In 2017, Elo is a sentence explaining why a [[bradley-terry-model|Bradley-Terry]] loss makes sense; in Constitutional AI it is the paper's principal y-axis, computed from crowdworker model-versus-model preferences.

children.name: The loss that never changed
children.narrative: A 1952 pairwise-comparison model supplies the preference-fitting loss in 2017 and is still supplying it, unchanged, underneath CAI's hybrid preference model.

children.name: Online training, inherited as an absence
children.narrative: The 2017 system refit its reward predictor continually; InstructGPT and CAI train on fixed comparison batches. CAI is the paper that names the regime as future work rather than practice (constitutional-ai, §"6.1 Future Directions", p. 15).

children.name: What AI labels unlock
children.narrative: The corpus's neatest closing loop: 2017's most human-expensive practice becomes cheap at the exact moment the labeler stops being human.

children.name: Everything downstream of a moving reward
children.narrative: The 2017 paper's coping machinery for a reward that changes during training, traced as one thread — the context that explains what CAI gave up by fixing its preference model, and what an automated online version would win back.

children.name: 2016: the open problem it carries furthest
children.narrative: Concrete Problems named scalable oversight as an open problem — safe behavior when the true objective is too costly to evaluate everywhere — and sketched remedies that all assumed the scarce resource was human labels. None of the sketches predicted AI feedback, which is what makes the lineage worth tracing: the reward model retroactively operationalized the problem in 2017, InstructGPT scaled it, and CAI takes the step the 2016 paper did not imagine, making the overseer itself a model. The 2016 paper's other bequest is a failure vocabulary: Goodhart's law, stated abstractly there, returns in CAI as concrete phenomena — evasiveness bred by a mislabeled proxy, and an over-trained RL-CAI turning accusatory.

children.name: The problem, six years on
children.narrative: Coined as an open problem in 2016, given a first mechanism in 2017, and stretched here to its furthest reading: the paper presents CAI as an extreme instance of using AI to help humans supervise AI (constitutional-ai, §"Scaling Supervision", p. 2).

children.name: Operationalized in hindsight
children.narrative: The one edge that touches all four papers: no paper in the chain announces that it solves scalable oversight, but read in sequence, the reward model is what the 2016 problem became.

children.name: The law it inherits
children.narrative: CAI inherits Goodhart's law as vocabulary and then instantiates it empirically: over-training against the preference model degrades true response quality while the score keeps climbing (constitutional-ai, §"4.3 Main Results", p. 12).

children.name: One law, named one instance at a time
children.narrative: The thread that follows the 2016 principle through InstructGPT's [[reward-overoptimization|over-optimization]] to CAI's evasiveness and over-trained harshness: each paper adds an instance, and none repeats one.

children.name: Evasiveness as a Goodhart case
children.narrative: CAI's founding grievance, filed under the 2016 law: crowdworkers rewarding harmlessness in isolation built a proxy whose cheapest maximizer was refusal.

children.name: Motifs the corpus repeats, with this paper as the newest instance
children.narrative: Some connections exist only when the four papers are read together, and Constitutional AI, as the latest paper, sits at the receiving end of most of them. The hindsight seams are edges no source paper states — 2016 principles fragmenting into 2022 phenomena. The assembly-line motif reads each pipeline stage's output as the next stage's engineered raw material, a logic CAI's critique-revise-finetune-RL chain follows exactly. The scale-asymmetry motif tracks small things supervising big ones, and CAI supplies its extreme case. And the paired-instruments motif — every primary metric shadowed by an independent check — is why CAI's Elo curves travel with an absolute harmfulness score.

children.name: Seams only hindsight can see
children.narrative: Edges flagged as connections no source paper draws, visible only by reading the corpus together; this paper appears in more of them than any other, usually as the 2022 phenomenon an earlier idea turns out to have been about.

children.name: Pipelines as assembly lines
children.narrative: Each stage's output is the next stage's engineered input. CAI contributes four links to the thread, from critique-and-revision feeding SL-CAI to the feedback model feeding the hybrid preference model.

children.name: Small supervises big
children.narrative: The corpus keeps finding wins that come from something small steering something large; CAI's contribution is the limiting case, a page of written principles standing in for tens of thousands of human labels.

children.name: Every metric gets a second instrument
children.narrative: A corpus habit of pairing each primary metric with an independently sourced check; CAI's Elo-plus-absolute-harmfulness pairing is the habit's latest instance.

stories.name: Constitutional AI and the big picture: the far rung of the oversight ladder
stories.intro:
Every paper in this corpus feeds a handful of larger claims — about who supervises the training, what the target of alignment is, and how optimization goes wrong. Constitutional AI feeds more of them than its size suggests, and the corpus's central claim ends on it: the ladder that runs from human demonstrations to human comparisons to AI feedback has this paper as its topmost tested rung.

The chapters below take the superthemes this paper contributes to, one at a time, and ask a narrower question than those pages answer: not what each big claim says, but what this paper specifically adds to it.
stories.narrative: Constitutional AI is where the corpus's central claim — that oversight can be delegated further and further without losing the human's intent — reaches its furthest tested point: it supplies the top rung of the scalable-oversight ladder, owns an entire supertheme about its method, sharpens the definition of the alignment target by attacking the tradeoff inside it, and hands the reward-hacking supertheme its newest empirical exhibits.

children.name: The oversight ladder, extended by one rung
children.narrative: The corpus's largest supertheme runs from a 2016 open problem through 2017's reward predictor to InstructGPT's industrial pipeline, and Constitutional AI is its current endpoint: the paper where the supervision itself, not just the reward, is produced by a model. Its contribution is not a new pipeline but a demonstration about the ladder's direction — each rung replaces a costlier form of human input with a cheaper, more scalable one, and this paper shows the replacement can reach the labels themselves while keeping human intent in a document humans can read and amend.

children.name: Scalable oversight made real
children.narrative: Constitutional AI's addition to this supertheme is its final chapter: after proposals (2016), a proof of concept (2017), and industrialization (InstructGPT), the human comparison data itself becomes the replaceable part.

children.name: The throughline itself
children.narrative: The corpus's most important thread, and this paper is its terminus: [[rlaif|RLAIF]], the [[feedback-model|feedback model]], and the [[hybrid-human-ai-preference-model|hybrid preference model]] are the concepts it adds.

children.name: The pipeline it rides on
children.narrative: This paper contributes no step to InstructGPT's three-step recipe — which is the point: its whole method fits inside the recipe's existing slots.

children.name: The drift problem it inherits
children.narrative: The 2017 countermeasures against a policy outrunning its reward model; Constitutional AI's cheap labels are what could make the online version of them routine.

children.name: The 2016 sketch it descends from
children.narrative: The remedy family where scalable oversight first got technical shape; the feedback model is the descendant none of the 2016 sketches predicted.

children.name: The supertheme it owns outright
children.narrative: One supertheme exists because this paper does: it gathers the constitution, the critique-revision loop, the feedback-model engineering, the red-team data sourcing, and the prior dialogue agents the paper measures itself against. What Constitutional AI adds here is everything — but the supertheme's real claim is subtler than a method summary. Written principles turn out to be a competitive interface for steering model behavior: cheaper than labels, more legible than weights, and auditable by anyone who can read a page.

children.name: Method and grounding
children.narrative: The paper's method, read as a claim about interfaces: a page of natural language can do the work of a labeled dataset, and can be audited in a way the dataset never could.

children.name: The supervised stage
children.narrative: Principles, critique, revision, and the ablations that justify each part — the half of the method that generates its own training data.

children.name: The labeler-engineering stage
children.narrative: The RL stage's counterpart problem: the prompting and calibration chain that makes a plain pretrained model into a usable preference labeler.

children.name: The human process it still needs
children.narrative: Adversarial prompts remain the one input the constitution cannot generate; this theme is the method's remaining human dependency.

children.name: The agents it argues against
children.narrative: [[lamda|LaMDA]], [[sparrow|Sparrow]], and [[context-distillation|context distillation]]: the prior systems against which the paper positions its claim that rules can live in a document rather than in a rule classifier.

children.name: Sharpening the target: helpful, harmless, and the tradeoff between them
children.narrative: The corpus's target-definition supertheme is mostly InstructGPT's: define instruction following, adopt helpful-honest-harmless, measure with preferences. Constitutional AI's addition is to attack the assumption hiding inside that definition — that helpfulness and harmlessness must be traded off. By showing the frontier can move outward, it turns the tradeoff from a fact about the target into a fact about the training data used to reach it. It also stress-tests the measurement half of the definition: Elo scores deliberately tuned so evasion loses points, cross-checked by an absolute harmfulness scale.

children.name: Defining the target
children.narrative: Constitutional AI keeps the HHH target and changes what counts as satisfying it: a refusal is no longer harmless by default, and the tradeoff between the aims is treated as an artifact to be engineered away.

children.name: The shared vocabulary, extended
children.narrative: The paper both inherits the HHH definition and extends its benchmark, using identification accuracy on HHH comparisons as the feasibility evidence for AI supervision.

children.name: The tradeoff attacked head-on
children.narrative: The paper's central empirical claim in full: the RLHF baselines, the Elo curves, and the Pareto argument that the frontier itself moved.

children.name: The measurement toolkit
children.narrative: This paper's contributions to the corpus's judgment-based measurement family: Elo as the primary instrument and the absolute harmfulness score as its independent check.

children.name: Where it appears in the margins
children.narrative: Three superthemes take smaller contributions from this paper. The reward-hacking supertheme, built mostly from the 2016 taxonomy, gains its newest empirical exhibits here: evasiveness and the over-trained, accusatory RL-CAI are Goodhart's law wearing 2022 clothes. The evaluation supertheme centered on InstructGPT shares one theme with this paper, the comparison-based measurement family both 2022 papers rely on. And the 2017 proof-of-concept supertheme touches Constitutional AI wherever the shared mechanism shows through: comparisons as the atomic unit of feedback, and a reward model that must be kept on distribution.

children.name: Reward hacking's newest exhibits
children.narrative: Constitutional AI's contribution here is evidence: two named, measured Goodhart instances inside a production-grade pipeline, six years after the law was stated abstractly.

children.name: The law's corpus-wide file
children.narrative: The theme that files this paper's evasiveness and over-training harshness alongside InstructGPT's over-optimization, all under the single 2016 principle.

children.name: The shared measurement apparatus
children.narrative: This InstructGPT-centered supertheme touches Constitutional AI through one theme, [[quality-measurement-methods|the judgment-based measurement family]], where the paper's Elo scores and absolute harmfulness scale sit alongside InstructGPT's [[win-rate|win rates]].

children.name: The proof of concept underneath
children.narrative: Constitutional AI touches the 2017 supertheme only where the shared mechanism shows through — and that is itself the finding: the proof of concept held up well enough that 2022 could build on it without revisiting it.

children.name: Comparisons, the surviving atom
children.narrative: Comparisons as the atomic unit of feedback: the one 2017 design decision this paper still depends on directly, whether the comparer is a human or a model.
